projects.title: How Fiber Optics Carry Internet Data
projects.prompt: Fiber-optic cable. Internet data. Laser. Core. Cladding. Total internal reflection. Photodetector.

lines.text: A fiber-optic cable carries internet data as flashes of light inside a strand of glass.
Instead of sending electrical pulses through copper, it guides light from one end to the other.
At the cable's transmitter, a laser or LED turns digital data into rapid pulses of light.
Those pulses enter the cable's narrow core, the central path reserved for the light.
The core is wrapped in cladding, which lets light reflect at the boundary instead of escaping.
Each pulse follows the fiber by repeated total internal reflection, even when the cable bends.
At the destination, a photodetector senses the arriving pattern of light and darkness.
The receiver converts that pattern back into electrical data for your computer or router.
So fiber-optic internet moves information by guiding coded light through glass, then decoding it at the far end.

scenes: The fiber confines and guides light

projects.title: How an Electric Motor Spins
projects.prompt: Electric motor. Magnetic field. Wire coil. Current. Torque. Shaft. Split-ring commutator. Brushes.

lines.text: An electric motor turns electrical energy into rotation to power fans, tools, and machines.
Inside the motor, the essential interaction is between electric current and a magnetic field.
Two fixed magnets create a magnetic field across the motor's central space.
A wire coil sits in that field, and the motor sends electric current through the coil.
Current in the coil produces opposite forces on its two sides, creating a turning force called torque.
Those forces rotate the coil and the shaft attached to it.
But the coil would stall if the current stayed in the same direction.
A split-ring commutator reverses the current every half turn, keeping the torque in the same rotational direction.
So the motor keeps spinning by repeatedly switching the coil's current so magnetic forces continue turning its shaft.

scenes: Current flows through the moving coil

projects.title: How a Transformer Changes Voltage
projects.prompt: Transformer. AC voltage. Primary coil. Secondary coil. Alternating magnetic field. Iron core. Induction. Turns ratio.

lines.text: A transformer changes AC voltage for the power grid and your home.
It transfers electrical energy between two coils without a direct wire connection.
Alternating current enters the primary coil, so its magnetic field continually changes.
The iron core guides this changing magnetic field around a closed loop.
The field then passes through the secondary coil on the other side.
Because the field keeps changing, it induces an alternating voltage in this second coil.
The number of wire turns controls the result.
More secondary turns increase voltage; fewer secondary turns decrease it.
So the transformer uses magnetic induction to change voltage while transferring power between its coils.

scenes: The core carries changing magnetic flux
The turns ratio sets the voltage

projects.title: How Radar Finds Distant Objects
projects.prompt: Radar. Radio pulse. Antenna. Aircraft. Echo. Round-trip time. Speed of light. Range. Rotating antenna.

lines.text: A radar finds distant objects by sending out radio waves and listening for their echoes.
This works in darkness because radio echoes do not need visible light.
The radar's transmitter creates a short radio pulse, and its antenna sends that pulse into space.
The pulse travels outward at the speed of light until it reaches an object such as an aircraft.
Some radio energy reflects from the aircraft and returns toward the radar antenna.
The radar measures the echo's round-trip time to calculate distance.
Multiplying half that time by the speed of light gives the object's range.
A rotating antenna repeats this process in different directions, building a map of echoes around the radar.
So radar locates objects by timing radio-wave echoes rather than relying on visible light.

scenes: Radar sends waves and receives echoes
The antenna launches a radio pulse
Repeated scans build an echo map

projects.title: How a Mechanical Watch Keeps Time
projects.prompt: Mechanical watch. Mainspring. Barrel. Gear train. Watch hands. Escapement. Balance wheel. Hairspring.

lines.text: A mechanical watch keeps time using stored spring energy instead of a battery.
Its clever mechanism releases that energy in tiny, evenly timed steps.
When you wind the watch, you tighten a mainspring inside a small drum called the barrel.
The mainspring slowly unwinds, turning the barrel and feeding energy into a series of gears.
This gear train carries rotation toward the watch hands while reducing the motion into useful speeds.
But left alone, the spring would release its energy much too quickly.
The escapement meters that energy, allowing the gears to advance one small step at a time.
A balance wheel oscillates back and forth at a steady rate, telling the escapement when each step may happen.
So the watch combines a steady oscillator, a controlled escapement, and gears to turn spring energy into accurate time.

scenes: A watch meters stored spring energy
The mainspring stores and releases energy
The gear train carries motion to the hands
The balance wheel sets a steady rhythm
